critique.good: The key column preserves every identifier, and all headers remain on one line. The four translation columns have a reasonably balanced rhythm, with no mid-word splits.
critique.problems: Several short translations wrap, and the shipping row breaks the English 3–5 range across lines. The Japanese email instruction occupies four lines, making that row noticeably tall.
critique.cause: The 115px English column has only 94px for text; the 120px Japanese column has 99px. The 100px Chinese column also forces the empty-cart phrase onto a second line.

critique.good: The wider English column keeps the confirmation and search strings on one line and preserves 3–5 in the shipping row. The key column and headers remain intact.
critique.problems: Arabic becomes a narrow, fragmented column: even short strings wrap, and the email instruction takes four lines. Chinese shipping text takes three lines. The extra English width does not reduce the overall table height.
critique.cause: English receives 140px, leaving only 84px for Arabic and 85px for Chinese. The Japanese and Arabic email translations still determine the tall email row.

critique.good: The 155px Japanese column keeps several short translations and the shipping string on one line. Arabic confirmation and empty-cart strings also fit on one line, while keys remain intact.
critique.problems: Chinese short strings wrap unnecessarily, and the English shipping string takes four lines. The resulting shipping row is taller, despite its Japanese translation fitting on one line.
critique.cause: The Japanese column takes width from English and Chinese, leaving them at 100px and 82px respectively; their usable text widths are only 79px and 61px.

critique.good: The keys remain intact, headers are clear, and the shared row heights keep translations associated. English and Arabic have relatively comfortable line breaks.
critique.problems: Japanese leaves a single character on the second line of the first translation and on the fourth line of the email message. Chinese and Arabic also make the shipping row three lines tall.
critique.cause: The 120px Japanese column is just too narrow for cleaner breaks in those cells. The 94px Chinese and 95px Arabic columns constrain the longer shipping translations.

critique.good: The 130px Japanese column keeps the first two translations on one line and reduces the email message to three lines. Keys and headers remain intact.
critique.problems: Arabic becomes noticeably fragmented, including two-line versions of short phrases and a four-line email message. The wider Japanese column therefore does not reduce the height of the longest row.
critique.cause: The extra Japanese width comes from reducing Arabic to 89px and Chinese to 90px; Arabic has only 68px of text space.

critique.good: Arabic reads more comfortably, with the first two translations on one line and the email message in three. The keys remain intact and the language columns retain a clear hierarchy.
critique.problems: The Japanese email message occupies four lines with awkward breaks, and the first Japanese translation wraps. The extra English width does not visibly improve the row heights.
critique.cause: Japanese has only 108px, while English receives 130px and still wraps the same phrases as in the other designs.

critique.good: The key column keeps every identifier intact, and the shaded first column makes rows easy to locate. All headers fit, and the four translations remain aligned across each row.
critique.problems: The Arabic shipping range is split across lines, making the number harder to read. The Japanese error message occupies four lines, while the Chinese shipping translation takes three.
critique.cause: At 107px, Arabic has only 86px of text space, which places the range at a line break. Japanese at 108px and Chinese at 94px are also narrow for their longer strings.

critique.good: The 101px Chinese column improves the shipping translation to two lines, and the Arabic number range stays together. Keys and headers remain intact.
critique.problems: The Arabic shipping translation now takes three lines, with a short final line. The Japanese error message still sets the height of the error row at four lines.
critique.cause: Seven pixels were moved from Arabic to Chinese: Arabic falls to 100px, leaving less room for the shipping phrase, while Japanese remains at 108px.

critique.good: The wider Japanese column gives that translation more horizontal space, and the Arabic number range stays together. The row identifiers remain intact.
critique.problems: Several Japanese cells end with a single character on a new line, including the confirmation and error messages. Chinese shipping returns to three lines, and Arabic shipping remains three lines.
critique.cause: Japanese at 119px changes the line breaks without reducing the tallest cell below four lines. Chinese at 90px and Arabic at 100px leave little room for their longer phrases.

understanding.purpose: A reference table for comparing checkout interface strings across four languages by translation key.
understanding.reading: Readers locate a key in the first column, then scan across the row to compare its translations; consistent row alignment helps keep those values associated.
groups: English, 中文, 日本語, and العربية are parallel translations of the same string and should remain easy to compare across each row.
Key is the row identifier and needs enough width to distinguish entries without breaking them.
keep_intact: Translation keys, including their dots and underscores.
Individual words and meaningful number ranges such as 3–5 where possible.
may_wrap: Longer English and Arabic phrases can wrap at word boundaries.
Chinese and Japanese text can wrap naturally between characters.
Short translations can use the height created by longer translations in the same row.

bad.why: The key column has only 149px of text space, forcing long identifiers to break or overflow and making the row labels harder to scan.

contrast.why: The key column has only 149px of text space, forcing long identifiers to break or overflow and making the row labels harder to scan.

final.rationale: r3A keeps every key intact and gives the four language columns a workable balance. Its final row fits in two lines across the translations, making that row easier to compare, although the Japanese error message still occupies four lines. r3B gives Japanese more room, but its narrower English column creates more wrapping, including a split across the shipping estimate.

general: Protect the readability of row identifiers because they anchor comparison across the table.
Allocate widths according to the content and writing systems, then judge the resulting line breaks across whole rows.
specific: The longest key needs 227px including padding and border to stay on one line.
In r3A, a modest increase in Chinese and Arabic width allows the shipping row to fit in two lines.

final.tradeoffs: r3B produces a more even maximum of three lines per cell and gives Japanese more comfortable breaks, while r3A preserves more useful English and Chinese line lengths. The other candidates remain publishable but distribute wrapping less favorably for this content.
final.uncertain: The ranges are approximate design tolerances, not browser-tested guarantees. They describe small changes around r3A with the remaining widths adjusted proportionally to stay within 661px; line breaks can change abruptly at particular widths.

A.why: The language columns have reasonable space, but most row identifiers break inside words, making the keys difficult to scan and copy.

B.why: Every key stays intact, and the language columns are reasonably balanced. The long Japanese error message wraps to four lines, but the rows remain easy to compare.

C.why: Keys stay intact and Arabic has useful space, but the narrow Chinese column creates cramped wrapping, including a single-character last line in the shipping row.

D.why: The language columns are comfortable, but every key breaks within an identifier. That weakens the row labels that readers need to locate strings.

E.why: Keys stay intact and Japanese has more room, but the narrow Arabic column forces several short lines; the shipping row also ends with a single Chinese character.

F.why: Keys remain intact and the columns are fairly balanced, but Chinese and Arabic shipping text wrap to three lines and the Japanese error message takes four.

reviews.unsure: B trades a four-line Japanese error message for more readable keys and generally balanced translations. The relative importance of keeping each language compact could change that preference.

A.why: All keys stay intact, and Japanese has enough room for several complete strings. The narrow Arabic column creates frequent wrapping, especially in the error and shipping rows.

B.why: Intact keys and a little more space for Chinese and Arabic make the table easy to scan. Japanese is cramped, with the error message ending in a line containing a single character.

C.why: The wider language columns reduce wrapping, but most keys break inside identifiers, making the row labels much harder to scan and copy.

D.why: Keys remain intact and Arabic has useful space, including for the shipping range. Chinese wraps tightly, and the Japanese error message ends with a single character.

E.why: Keys remain intact, but the narrow Japanese and Arabic columns produce several short lines; the shipping row is particularly fragmented across Chinese and Arabic.

F.why: The language columns have a comfortable rhythm, but every key breaks inside an identifier, substantially weakening the row labels.

reviews.unsure: B and D are close: D gives Arabic more room, while B gives Chinese and Japanese slightly more space. The best balance depends on which language readers compare most often.
